flexiSDM

2026 TWS

2026-11-03

1 Introduction

This vignette walks you through fitting an integrated species distribution model (iSDM) using the SpFut.flexiSDM package. We work with a fictional species—the Great Salt Lake Cyclops—to demonstrate how to integrate multiple datasets into a single model.

1.1 Learning objectives

By the end of this workshop you will be able to:

  1. Define a study region with associated environmental covariates
  2. Set up and fit an integrated SDM in NIMBLE via SpFut.flexiSDM
  3. Summarize and visualize model output
  4. Compare model estimates against known truth

2 Prerequisites

Confirm that you have the correct package version installed. This package is stored on GitLab, NOT CRAN, so you need to use remotes::install_git() rather than install.packages().

remotes::install_git("https://code.usgs.gov/eastern-ecological-science-center/nearmi/SpFut-flexiSDM.git", force = T)

packageVersion("SpFut.flexiSDM") == "1.1.3"

Load the packages used throughout and set a seed for reproducibility.

library(tidyverse)
library(SpFut.flexiSDM)

set.seed(1)

3 Understanding the inputs

We begin from pre-built data. The section Simulate data at the end of this tutorial demonstrates how to simulate the data.

load("TWS2026/data/data.RData", verbose = TRUE)
#> Loading objects:
#>   region
#>   datalist
#>   species.data
#>   covar
#>   true

3.1 The region

A region object has four components. It can be created by make_region() (real species) or format_sim() (simulated species).

Component What it is
range Boundary used to build the study region (NULL for simulated range)
region Outer boundary of the study region
sp.grid Spatial analysis units (here, 25 km² hexbins)
boundary Where the region is cut off (can differ from region) 
# For a simulated species, range is NULL
region$range
#> NULL

# Outer boundary of the study region
ggplot(region$region) + geom_sf()


# sp.grid holds the spatial units for analysis (25 km2 hexbins)
ggplot(region$sp.grid) + geom_sf()

nrow(region$sp.grid)
#> [1] 3213

# conus.grid.id is a unique label for each hexbin
head(region$sp.grid)

# boundary dictates where the region is cut off
# (here identical to region, but it could be e.g. a state boundary)
ggplot(region$boundary) + geom_sf()

Note. conus.grid.id is the key that links every dataset, covariate, and output back to a specific hexbin.

3.2 Species data

The species.data object (from load_species_data() or format_sim()) has two elements:

  • locs — where each data point sits in discrete (disc, assigned to a hexbin) and continuous (cont, coordinates) space. This is useful for mapping.
  • obs — a list where each element holds date, location, and count info for one dataset.
head(species.data$locs$disc)
head(species.data$locs$cont)

# Overlay observation locations on the region, colored by source
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = region$region) +
  geom_sf(data = species.data$locs$cont, aes(color = source))

# Peek at each dataset
head(species.data$obs$iNat)   # presence-only
head(species.data$obs$NSLBB)  # detection / non-detection
head(species.data$obs$UMCC)   # count
head(species.data$obs$SLCBS)  # count, repeated visits

Visualize everything together with map_species_data().

map_species_data(title = "Simulated data",
                 region = region,
                 plot = "samples",
                 sim = TRUE,
                 details = TRUE,
                 species.data = species.data,
                 inat.agg = FALSE,
                 plot.range = FALSE,
                 plot.region = TRUE,
                 subtitle = FALSE,
                 out = NULL)$plot
#> Using real map features

3.3 Covariates

Environmental covariates live in a data frame (covar) with conus.grid.id that matches region$sp.grid. Values must already be scaled, and quadratic terms must be pre-squared.

# Linear + quadratic covariates for the ecological process
covs.z  <- c("wetland", "footprint", "S", "elevation", "elevation2")

# Covariates for the presence-only (iNat) observation process.
# Because PO data are modeled at the hexbin level, these must also live in covar.
covs.PO <- c("effort")


head(covar)
gridcovar <- full_join(region$sp.grid, covar, by = "conus.grid.id")

ggplot(gridcovar) + geom_sf(aes(fill = wetland))

ggplot(gridcovar) + geom_sf(aes(fill = elevation))

Attach labels, then plot the covariates and check correlations.

cov.labs <- data.frame(
  covariate = names(covar),
  Label = c("conus.grid.id", "Wetland", "Footprint", "Elevation",
            "Elevation^2", "South", "Effort")) %>%
  filter(covariate != "conus.grid.id")

cov.labs
plot_covar(covar = covar, 
           region = region, 
           cov.labs = cov.labs, 
           scaled = TRUE)$plot


cor_covar(covar = covar, 
          cov.labs = cov.labs, 
          color.threshold = 0.25)$plot

Checkpoint. Highly correlated covariates (flagged by cor_covar()) can destabilize estimates. Inspect the correlation plot before proceeding.

4 Setting up model components

4.1 The gridkey and cross-validation

The gridkey maps hexbins to NIMBLE indices and assigns each to a "test" or "train" group. We first generate spatial blocks for cross-validation.

# k = number of folds the blocks are grouped into
spatblocks <- make_CV_blocks(region, rows = 5, cols = 5, k = 3)

head(spatblocks)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = spatblocks, aes(fill = as.factor(folds))) +
  geom_sf(data = region$region, fill = NA)

Choose which fold to hold out. "none" uses all data for training.

fold.out <- "none"
gridkey  <- make_gridkey(region, spatblocks, fold.out = fold.out)

head(gridkey)

# Visualize the train/test split
key <- full_join(region$sp.grid, gridkey, by = "conus.grid.id")
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = key, aes(fill = group))

Try it. Set fold.out = 1 and re-plot. The cells in fold 1 become test data; to evaluate predictive performance, you could predict intensity in these cells and then compare the predicted values to the truth.

gridkey1 <- make_gridkey(region, spatblocks, fold.out = 1, method = "overlap")

key1 <- full_join(region$sp.grid, gridkey1, by = "conus.grid.id")
ggplot() + geom_sf(data = key1, aes(fill = group))

4.2 Spatial random effect

The ICAR spatial random effect can be estimated on a coarse grid to cut runtime: rather than one random effect per hexbin, effects are estimated per group of hexbins.

spatRegion <- suppressWarnings(make_spatkey(region$sp.grid))

# spatkey maps each conus.grid.id to a spat.grid.id
spatRegion$spatkey[1:10,]

# spatgrid is an sf object containing the coarse grid
head(spatRegion$spat.grid)
ggplot(spatRegion$spat.grid) + geom_sf()

For this vignette we estimate without the coarse grid, so set spatRegion to NULL.

spatRegion <- NULL

5 Building the NIMBLE model

5.1 Describe your datasets with file.info

Each dataset needs a row describing its type and detection covariates.

Field Meaning
file.label Must match names(species.data$obs)
data.type "PO", "DND", or "count"
covar.mean Detection covariate(s) averaged across passes
covar.sum Detection covariate(s) summed across passes
PO.extent "CONUS" or a two-letter state code (NA for non-PO) 
file.info <- data.frame(file.label = c("iNat", "NSLBB", "UMCC", "SLCBS"),
                        data.type  = c("PO",   "DND",   "count", "count"),
                        covar.mean = c("effort", "cov.siteA", "cov.siteA", "cov.siteA"),
                        covar.sum  = c(NA, NA, NA, NA),
                        PO.extent  = c("CONUS", NA, NA, NA))

file.info

5.2 Format species data for NIMBLE

The species data are formatted into data and constants, which eventually go into NIMBLE.

sp.data <- sppdata_for_nimble(species.data = species.data,
                              region = region,
                              covar = covar,
                            
                              # things defined earlier
                              file.info = file.info,
                              covs.PO = covs.PO,
                              keep.conus.grid.id = gridkey$conus.grid.id[gridkey$group == "train"],
                            
                              # which observation models to use
                              occ.mod = TRUE,
                              nmix.mod = TRUE,
                              min.visits.incl = 3,
                            
                              # these options only apply to real data; see the companion vignette
                              stategrid = NULL,
                              statelines.rm = FALSE)

5.3 Combine with the ecological process

The environmental data for the region is added to the formatted species data. This section also sets up the spatial autocorrelation portion of the model. The output is a single data and constants that are ready for NIMBLE.

tmp <- data_for_nimble(sp.data = sp.data,
                       covar = covar,
                       covs.z = covs.z,
                       sp.auto = TRUE,       # spatial autocorrelation
                       coarse.grid = FALSE,
                       region = region,
                       gridkey = gridkey,
                       spatRegion = NULL)

data      <- tmp$data
constants <- tmp$constants

5.4 Generate code, initial values, and parameters

nimble_code() writes the NIMBLE model from the information in data and constants. The same inputs generate initial values and the vector of parameters to monitor.

code <- nimble_code(data = data,
                    constants = constants,
                    path = tempdir(),
                    block.out = fold.out,
                    Bprior = "dnorm(0,1)",        # prior on coefficients
                    
                    # spatial model parameters
                    sp.auto = TRUE,
                    coarse.grid = FALSE,
                    zero_mean = TRUE,
                    tau = 1,
                    
                    # observation model
                    min.visits.incl = 3,
                    occ.mod = TRUE,
                    nmix.mod = TRUE)
#> 
#> # Process Model
#> 
#> # 3213 cells
#> for (i in 1:nCell) {
#> 
#>     # log intensity
#>     XB0[i] <- inprod(B[1:nCovZ], Xz[i,1:nCovZ])
#>     log(lambda0[i]) <- XB0[i] + spat[i] # residual spatial effect
#> 
#> }
#> 
#> 
#> # ---------------------------------------
#> 
#> # Observation Model 1: PO, iNat
#> # 3213 cells
#> for (j in 1:nW1) {
#> 
#>   # Make dataset-specific lambda
#>   lambdaD1[j] <- lambda0[Wcells1[j]] * alpha[1]
#> 
#>   # Observation model
#>   W1[j] ~ dpois(lambdaD1[j] * E1[j]) # Poisson
#> 
#>   # Effort 
#>   log(E1[j]) <- A1[1] * Xw1[j,1]
#> 
#>   # Prior for X imputation
#>   Xw1[j, 1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
#> }
#> 
#>   
#> 
#> # Observation Model 2: DND, NSLBB
#> # 78 observations, 1 median visits per site
#> for (j in 1:nV2) {
#> 
#>   # Make dataset-specific lambda
#>   lambdaD2[j] <- lambda0[Vcells2[j]] * alpha[2]
#> 
#>   # Observation model
#>   V2[j] ~ dbern(1-exp(-lambdaD2[j] * p2[j])) # Bernoulli
#> 
#>   # Detection 
#>   log(p2[j]) <- D2[1] * Xv2[j,1]
#> 
#>   # Prior for X imputation
#>   Xv2[j, 1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
#> }
#> 
#>   
#> 
#> # Observation Model 3: count, UMCC
#> # 40 observations, 1 median visits per site
#> for (j in 1:nY3) {
#> 
#>   # Make dataset-specific lambda
#>   lambdaD3[j] <- lambda0[Ycells3[j]] * alpha[3]
#> 
#>   # Observation model
#>   Y3[j] ~ dpois(lambdaD3[j] * p3[j]) # Poisson
#> 
#>   # Detection 
#>   log(p3[j]) <- C3[1] * Xy3[j,1]
#> 
#>   # Prior for X imputation
#>   Xy3[j, 1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
#> }
#> 
#>   
#> 
#> # Observation Model 4: count, SLCBS
#> # 120 observations, 10 median visits per site
#> 
#> # Site-level latent state
#> for (s in 1:nSitesY4) {
#>   lambdaD4[s] <- lambda0[Ycells4[s]] * alpha[4]
#>   ND4[s] ~ dpois(lambdaD4[s])
#> }
#> 
#> # Visit-level observations
#> for (j in 1:nY4) {
#> 
#>   # Observation model
#>   Y4[j] ~ dbinom(p4[j], ND4[siteY4[j]]) # N-mixture
#> 
#>   # Detection 
#>   logit(p4[j]) <- inprod(C4[1:nCovY4], Xy4[j,1:nCovY4])
#> 
#>   # Prior for X imputation
#>   for (c in 1:nCovY4) {
#>     Xy4[j,c] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
#>   }
#> }
#> 
#>   
#> # ---------------------------------------
#> # Process priors
#> for (a in 1:nCovZ) {
#>   B[a] ~ dnorm(0,1)
#> }
#> 
#> # Dataset intercepts
#> for (a in 1:nD) {
#>   alpha[a] <- exp(w[a])
#>   w[a] ~ dnorm(0,1)
#> }
#> 
#> # Observation priors, PO 1: iNat
#> for (b in 1:nCovW1) {
#>   A1[b] ~ dnorm(0,1)
#> }
#> 
#> # Observation priors, DND 2: NSLBB
#> for (b in 1:nCovV2) {
#>   D2[b] ~ dnorm(0,1)
#> }
#> 
#> # Observation priors, count 3: UMCC
#> for (b in 1:nCovY3) {
#>   C3[b] ~ dnorm(0,1)
#> }
#> 
#> # Observation priors, count 4: SLCBS
#> for (b in 1:nCovY4) {
#>   C4[b] ~ dnorm(0,1)
#> }
#> 
#> tau <- 1
#> spat[1:nCell] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:nCell], tau, zero_mean = 1)

inits <- function(x) {
  nimble_inits(data = data,
               constants = constants,
               sp.auto = TRUE,
               min.visits.incl = 3,
               occ.mod = TRUE,
               nmix.mod = TRUE,
               seed = x)
}

params <- nimble_params(data = data,
                        constants = constants,
                        lambda = TRUE,
                        XB = TRUE,
                        sp.auto = TRUE,
                        effort = FALSE)

6 Fitting the model

Workshop tip. These settings keep runtime short for a live session. For real analyses, increase iter substantially and confirm convergence before interpreting results.

iter   <- 5000
thin   <- 5
burnin <- floor(iter * 0.75)

samples <- nimbleParallel(code = code,
                          data = data,
                          constants = constants,
                          inits = inits,
                          param = params,
                          iter = iter,
                          burnin = burnin,
                          thin = thin)
#> Jack be NIMBLE... 
#> Jack be quick... 
#> Jack jumped over the candlestick!

# Derive quantities (occupancy and projections) from the raw samples
samples <- lapply(samples, get_derived,
                  data = data,
                  
                  # this is where you would add projections, if there were new X data to project to in `data`
                  project = 0,
                  proj.data = data,
                  
                  sp.auto = TRUE,
                  coarse.grid = FALSE,
                  spatRegion = spatRegion)

# Summarize across chains
out <- summarize_samples(samples = samples,
                         data = data,
                         constants = constants,
                         project = 0,
                         coarse.grid = FALSE,
                         block.out = fold.out,
                         gridkey = gridkey,
                         effort = FALSE,
                         cores = 2L)
#> Summarizing chains using 2 cores...
#> Time difference of 1.5862 mins
#> Chain summarization complete

If fitting fails or time runs short, load the pre-computed output.

if (!exists("out")) load("TWS2026/data/output.RData")

7 Inspecting results

7.1 Convergence and coefficients

Always check chains before interpreting estimates.

# Process (beta) coefficients
plot_chains(samples, 
            data = data, 
            cov.labs = cov.labs, 
            plot = "B", 
            cutoff = 0)$plot


plot_pars(out = out$process.coef, 
          cov.labs = cov.labs)$plot


plot_effects(data = data, 
             out = out, 
             cov.labs = cov.labs, 
             unscale_covar = TRUE)$plot

# Dataset intercepts (alpha)
plot_chains(samples, 
            data = data, 
            constants = constants,
            cov.labs = cov.labs, 
            plot = "alpha", 
            cutoff = 0)$plot


plot_pars(out = out$alpha, 
          cov.labs = cov.labs)$plot

# Observation coefficients
plot_chains(samples, 
            data = data, 
            constants = constants,
            cov.labs = cov.labs, 
            plot = "observation", 
            cutoff = 0)$plot


plot_pars(out = out$obs.coef, 
          cov.labs = cov.labs)$plot

Checkpoint. Look for well-mixed, overlapping chains (“fuzzy caterpillars”). Poor mixing means you need more iterations. Sometimes, poor mixing can also be a sign of insufficient data.

7.2 Map predictions

# Relative abundance (intensity)
map_species_data(title = "Estimated intensity",
                 region = region, out = out, sim = TRUE,
                 plot = "lambda", plot.range = FALSE, plot.region = TRUE)$plot
#> Using real map features

# Occupancy probability
map_species_data(title = "Estimated occupancy probability",
                 region = region, out = out, sim = TRUE,
                 plot = "psi", plot.range = FALSE, plot.region = TRUE)$plot
#> Using real map features

8 Comparing estimates to truth

Because this is simulated, we know the true parameters. Use sim_compare() to evaluate recovery. Most flexiSDM plotting functions return a list with $plot (a ggplot object) and $data (the underlying data frame).

names(datalist) <- names(species.data$obs)

tmp <- sim_compare(out, true = true, plot = "process")
tmp$plot

tmp$data

sim_compare(out, true = true, plot = "process")$plot  # process coefficients

sim_compare(out, true = true, plot = "lambda")$plot   # intensity

sim_compare(out, true = true, plot = "spat")$plot     # spatial effect


sim_compare(out, true = datalist, plot = "alpha")$plot  # intercepts

sim_compare(out, true = datalist, plot = "obs")$plot    # observation params

Discussion. How close are the estimates to the “truth”? Which parameters are recovered well, and which are uncertain?

9 Why we need data integration

The central motivation for iSDMs is that combining datasets generally beats using any one alone. We demonstrate this by comparing the integrated model against models fit to each dataset separately. Pre-computed single-dataset outputs are provided.

load("TWS2026/data/model-outputs.RData", verbose = TRUE)
#> Loading objects:
#>   all.proc
#>   all.alph
#>   all.lamb
#>   all.obs
#>   all.spat

9.1 Compare process parameters

Look for the "all" model producing estimates closer to truth with tighter intervals than the single-dataset models.

proc <- sim_compare(out, 
                    true = true, 
                    plot = "process")$dat %>%
        mutate(model = "all")  # label the integrated model

all.proc <- bind_rows(all.proc, proc)   # add to single-dataset results

ggplot(all.proc) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = true), color = "darkblue",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.75) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(x = covariate, y = mean, ymin = lo, ymax = hi,
                      color = model, group = model),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  facet_wrap(~ covariate, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw()

9.2 Compare intensity estimates

The best predictions fall closest to the 1-to-1 line.

lamb <- sim_compare(out, true = true, plot = "lambda")$dat %>%
          mutate(model = "all")
all.lamb <- bind_rows(all.lamb, lamb)

# Estimated vs. true
ggplot(all.lamb) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = true, y = mean, color = model)) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, scales = "free") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 50), ylim = c(0, 50)) +
  theme_bw()

9.3 Map intensity and error

all.lamb.sf <- region$sp.grid %>%
  full_join(all.lamb, by = "conus.grid.id")

# Truncate extreme values for a readable color scale
q90 <- quantile(all.lamb.sf$mean, 0.90)
all.lamb.sf$mean[all.lamb.sf$mean > q90] <- q90

# Estimated intensity by model
ggplot(all.lamb.sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mean, color = mean)) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(option = "magma") +
  viridis::scale_color_viridis(option = "magma")


# Deviation from truth (blue = under, red = over)
ggplot(all.lamb.sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mean - true, color = mean - true)) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_fill_gradient2() +
  scale_color_gradient2()

Discussion. Which single-dataset models show the largest spatial bias? Where does integration help most—and why might that relate to where each dataset was collected?

Check your understanding.

  • Compared to single-dataset models, what do we expect from an integrated SDM?
  • Which single-dataset model performs best, and which performs worst? Why?
  • Why should you always inspect the chains before interpreting estimates?

10 Appendix: Simulate data

For reference, the workshop data were generated with the workflow below. You do not need to run this during the workshop—the pre-built data.RData is loaded at the start—but it clarifies why the datasets differ and provides a template if you want to simulate your own species.

A single true species distribution is simulated from scaled covariates plus a small spatial field. Four datasets are then drawn from that one truth, each mimicking a real-world sampling style:

Dataset Type Sampling design
iNat Presence-only (sim_POdat) Opportunistic; effort correlated with footprint
NSLBB Detection/non-detection 100 sites randomly placed around the nothern part of the Great Salt Lake, 1 visit
UMCC Count (sim_surveydat) 50 sites spaced throughout Utah, 1 visit
SLCBS Count (sim_surveydat) 20 sites randomly placed near Salt Lake City, 10 visits

Each dataset covers a different region and carries different biases— exactly the situation integrated SDMs are built to exploit.

10.1 Setup

The simulation uses a few extra packages—SpFut.covariates for downloading environmental layers, rnaturalearth for map data, and sf for spatial operations.

library(SpFut.flexiSDM)
# remotes::install_git("https://code.usgs.gov/eastern-ecological-science-center/nearmi/SpFut-covariates.git")
library(SpFut.covariates)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

10.2 Defining the region

We anchor the study area on real geography: the Great Salt Lake (GSL) and Salt Lake City (SLC). These are pulled from Natural Earth. The lake becomes the species’ core range, and the city is used later to place an urban survey dataset.

# Great Salt Lake
GSL <- ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes",
                   category = "physical", returnclass = "sf") %>%
        filter(name == "Great Salt Lake")

# Salt Lake City point
slc_point <- ne_download(scale = 10, type = "populated_places",
                         category = "cultural", returnclass = "sf") %>%
              filter(NAME == "Salt Lake City")

# Salt Lake City outline: the urban area polygon that contains the SLC point
urban <- ne_download(scale = 10, type = "urban_areas",
                     category = "cultural", returnclass = "sf") %>%
          st_transform(st_crs(slc_point))
SLC <- urban[st_intersects(urban, slc_point, sparse = FALSE), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = GSL, fill = "blue") +
  geom_sf(data = SLC, fill = "brown")

We buffer the lake by 100 km, then lay down a hexagonal grid. The hexagon size is computed from the target cell area (25 km²). Finally, make_region() packages the range, buffer, and grid into the region object.

# use Great Salt Lake as starting area, add buffer
buffer <- 100000
gridstart <- GSL %>%
              st_transform(crs = 3857) %>%
              st_buffer(buffer)

# create grid
cellarea <- 25e6  # hexbins with 25km2 area -- smaller would raise runtime a lot
cellsize <- 2 * sqrt(cellarea/((3*sqrt(3)/2))) * sqrt(3)/2 # length across hexagon
conus.grid <- st_make_grid(gridstart, cellsize = cellsize, square = F) %>%
              st_as_sf() %>% 
              rename(geometry = x) %>% 
              mutate(conus.grid.id = 1:nrow(.))

# create region
region <- make_region(rangelist = list(lake = GSL),
                      buffer = buffer,
                      grid = conus.grid)
#> Removing small cells
#> Removing cells with <=1 neighbor...

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = region$sp.grid) +
  geom_sf(data = GSL, fill = "blue") +
  geom_sf(data = SLC, fill = "brown")

10.3 Building covariates

Real environmental layers (landcover, human footprint, elevation) are downloaded for each hexbin via the SpFut.covariates helpers. We keep wetland, water, elevation, footprint, and a south-facing indicator (S).

land <- get_landcover(locs = region$sp.grid, 
                      path = "TWS2026/data/", 
                      id.label = "conus.grid.id")
footprint <- get_footprint(locs = region$sp.grid, 
                           id.label = "conus.grid.id")
elev <- get_elevation(locs = region$sp.grid, 
                      path = "TWS2026/data/", 
                      id.label = "conus.grid.id")

# join covariates
covar <- full_join(land, footprint, by = "conus.grid.id") %>%
          full_join(elev, by = "conus.grid.id") %>%
          select(conus.grid.id, wetland, water, elevation, footprint, S) %>%
          rename(grid.id = conus.grid.id)
covar$wetland[which(covar$wetland > 0.5)] <- 0.5 # lower extreme wetland values to help model run better

Recall the modeling requirement that covariates be scaled. Here we save an unscaled copy, then scale all numeric columns with scale_this()—the same convention the fitting workflow expects.

covar_unscaled <- covar

# scale numeric cols
numcols <- sapply(covar, is.numeric)
numcols <- which(numcols)
covar[,numcols] <- sapply(covar[,numcols], scale_this)

summary(covar)

# visualize covariates
covlabs <- data.frame(covariate = c("wetland", "elevation", "footprint", "S"),
                      Label = c("Wetland", "Elevation", "Footprint", "South-facing"))

plot_covar(rename(covar, 
                  conus.grid.id = grid.id),
                  region,
                  cov.labs = covlabs,
                  scaled = T)$plot

cor_covar(rename(covar, 
                 conus.grid.id = grid.id),
                 covlabs)$plot

10.4 Simulating the true species

Now we define the “truth.” We choose a coefficient for each covariate—these are the values the fitted model will try to recover—and add the quadratic elevation2 term. A small spatial field (spat) adds autocorrelated noise; dividing by 10,000 keeps it small relative to the covariate effects (XB).

# Specify parameters
covs.z <- c("wetland", "footprint", "elevation", "elevation2", "S")
params <- c(0.46, -0.34, 0.27, -0.06, -0.21)
names(params) <- covs.z

# create quadratic term
covar <- covar %>%
          mutate(elevation2 = elevation * elevation) %>%
          select(all_of(c("grid.id", covs.z)))

# rename grid.id
grid <- region$sp.grid %>% rename(grid.id = conus.grid.id)

# create spatial noise
# we want this to be small compared to XB, so divide it by 10000
spat <- data.frame(grid.id = grid$grid.id,
                   spat = sim_cov(locs = grid, range = 100000)/10000)
summary(spat$spat)

With parameters and spatial field in hand, sim_species() produces the true intensity surface, which we compare against later.

# put together use list
use <- list(grid.sim = grid,
            grid.inf = grid,
            covar = covar,
            param = params,
            spat = spat)

# simulate species!
sp <- sim_species(use = use)

map_species_data(title = "Simulated species",
                 plot  = "true",
                 sim   = sp)$plot

summary(sp$true$intensity)

10.5 Simulating the datasets

From one true distribution we draw four datasets of different types and with different biases.

10.5.1 iNat (presence-only)

Presence-only data mimic opportunistic citizen-science records. We build an effort surface that is loosely correlated with human footprint plus noise, then sim_POdat() generates presences where both the species and observer effort are high.

# Create effort metric - slightly correlated with human footprint but lots of noise
effort <- (sim_cov(locs = grid, range = 10) + footprint$footprint/10)

ggplot(grid) + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill = effort))

# create use list
covar.eff <- data.frame(grid.id = grid$grid.id,
                        effort = scale(effort))
param <- c("effort" = 3.06)

use <- list(covar = covar.eff, param = param, alpha = 0.01)

# simulate
start <- Sys.time()
inat <- sim_POdat(true      = sp,
                  use       = use,
                  cell.area = 0.005)

Sys.time() - start
nrow(inat$dat)

10.5.2 Northern Salt Lake Beast Brigade (detection/non-detection)

A structured survey covering only the northern part of the region (above 41.2° latitude). We crop to that area, place 100 random sites, and sim_surveydat() generates detection/non-detection records. Note the restricted spatial extent—this is a deliberate bias the integrated model must handle.

# start with GSL, add buffer, then crop to above 41.2 lat
buffGSL <- GSL %>%
  st_transform(3857) %>% st_buffer(80000) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

cropbb <- buffGSL %>% st_bbox()
cropbb["ymin"] <- 41.2
northGSL <- st_crop(buffGSL, cropbb)

# find grid cells in that region
northGSLgrid <- st_intersection(st_transform(region$sp.grid, 4326), northGSL) %>%
                select(conus.grid.id, geometry) %>%
                rename(grid.id = conus.grid.id)

# create locations within that region
locs <- sim_survey_sites(grid = st_transform(northGSLgrid, 3857),
                         method = "random", nsite = 100, nvisit = 1)

# visualize
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = region$sp.grid, aes(fill = sp$true$intensity, 
                                     color = sp$true$intensity)) +
  geom_sf(data = northGSLgrid, fill = NA, color = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = northGSL, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  geom_sf(data = locs, color = "green")

# create use list
use <- list(locs = locs)

# simulate
NSLBB <- sim_surveydat(true      = sp,
                       use       = use,
                       survey.type = "DND",
                       covFormSite = "linear",
                       covFormVisit = "")

10.5.3 Utah Mythical Creature Count (count)

A count survey on a regular grid of 50 sites within Utah (below 42° latitude). Counts carry more information than detection/non-detection, but coverage is spatially limited and the sites are very spread out.

grid1 <- region$region %>% st_transform(crs = 4326)
cropbb <- grid1 %>% st_bbox()
cropbb["ymax"] <- 42

grid1 <- st_crop(grid1, cropbb) %>%
          st_intersection(st_transform(region$sp.grid, 4326), 
                          region$sp.grid) %>%
          select(conus.grid.id, geometry) %>%
          rename(grid.id = conus.grid.id)

locs <- sim_survey_sites(grid = st_transform(grid1, 3857),
                         method = "regular", nsite = 50, nvisit = 1)

use <- list(locs = locs)

UMCC <- sim_surveydat(use = use,
                      true      = sp,
                      survey.type = "count",
                      covFormSite = "linear",
                      covFormVisit = "")

10.5.4 SLC Biodiversity Survey (count, repeated visits)

An intensive local survey near Salt Lake City: only 20 sites, but each visited 10 times. Repeated visits let the model separate detection probability from true abundance—rich information over a tiny footprint.

# start with SLC, add buffer
SLCgrid <- SLC %>%
            st_transform(3857) %>% st_buffer(10000) %>%
            st_transform(4326) %>%
            st_intersection(st_transform(region$sp.grid, 4326)) %>%
            select(conus.grid.id, geometry) %>%
            rename(grid.id = conus.grid.id)

# create use list
locs <- sim_survey_sites(grid = st_transform(SLCgrid, 3857),
                         method = "random", nsite = 20, nvisit = 10)

use <- list(locs = locs)

# simulate
SLCBS <- sim_surveydat(true         = sp,
                       use          = use,
                       survey.type  = "count",
                       covFormSite  = "linear",
                       covFormVisit = "",
                       link         = "logit")

Check your understanding. Each dataset trades off coverage against information content: iNat is broad but biased, NSLBB and UMCC are structured but spatially restricted, and SLCBS is information-rich but tiny. No single one sees the whole picture, which is why integrating them is critical.

10.6 Formatting and saving

Finally, the four datasets are collected into a named list and passed to format_sim(), which returns the region, species.data, and covar objects in the shape the fitting workflow expects. We also save a couple of reference maps and strip covForm from the truth object for compatibility with flexiSDM v1.1.1, then save everything to data.RData—the file loaded at the start of this vignette.

datalist <- list(PO_iNat = inat,
                 DND_NSLBB = NSLBB,
                 count_UMCC = UMCC,
                 count_SLCBS = SLCBS)
sim_out <- format_sim(true = sp,
                      data = datalist)

region       <- sim_out$region
species.data <- sim_out$species.data
covar        <- sim_out$covar

# Add effort covariates for PO to covar
covar <- full_join(covar, datalist$PO_iNat$covar, by = c("conus.grid.id" = "grid.id"))


pl <- map_species_data(title = "Simulated data",
                       region = region,
                       plot = "samples",
                       sim = T,
                       details = T,
                       species.data = species.data,
                       inat.agg = FALSE,
                       plot.range = FALSE,
                       plot.region = TRUE,
                       subtitle = FALSE)$plot

pl <- map_species_data(title = "True distribution",
                       region = region,
                       plot = "true",
                       sim = sp)$plot

true <- sp
# true$covForm <- NULL # remove covForm so that it works with flexiSDM v1.1.1

save(region, datalist, species.data, covar, true,
     file = "TWS2026/data/data.RData")
